sectionTitle: Waves in air, fluids and solids — part 4.6.1.1

specStatements.text: Waves may be either transverse or longitudinal.
The ripples on a water surface are an example of a transverse wave.
Longitudinal waves show areas of compression and rarefaction. Sound waves travelling through air are longitudinal.
Students should be able to describe the difference between longitudinal and transverse waves.
Students should be able to describe evidence that, for both ripples on a water surface and sound waves in air, it is the wave and not the water or air itself that travels.

concepts.definition: A travelling oscillation that carries energy from one place to another without the material it passes through being carried along. Waves may be either transverse or longitudinal.
A wave in which the oscillations are at right angles (perpendicular) to the direction in which the wave travels.
A wave in which the oscillations are along (parallel to) the direction in which the wave travels.
The standard example of a transverse wave. The surface of the water oscillates up and down while the ripple itself travels outwards across the surface, at right angles to that up-and-down movement.
A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles are pushed closer together than normal, so the density and the pressure there are higher than normal.
A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles are spread further apart than normal, so the density and the pressure there are lower than normal.
A longitudinal wave. A vibrating source such as a loudspeaker cone pushes and pulls the air next to it, sending a series of compressions and rarefactions travelling out through the air.
Each particle of the material vibrates to and fro about one position and returns to it. The particle does not travel along with the wave; it only passes the disturbance on to its neighbours.

concepts.term: Direction of travel of the wave
concepts.definition: The direction in which the wave itself moves away from the source. A wave is classified as transverse or longitudinal by comparing the direction of the oscillations with this direction, not with 'up and down' or 'sideways'.

A cork or polystyrene ball floating in a ripple tank bobs up and down in the same place as ripples pass beneath it, instead of being carried to the far side. The ripple crosses the tank; the water does not.

A loudspeaker can be heard right across a room, yet no draught of air arrives with the sound and the air by the loudspeaker is never used up. The sound wave crosses the room; the air itself only vibrates in place.

misconceptions.question: When ripples travel across a pond, what happens to the water?
misconceptions.correct: Each part of the surface moves up and down as the ripple passes, and stays where it is.
misconceptions.misconception: The water travels along with the ripple, so water from the middle of the pond ends up at the bank.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ripples look like moving humps of water, and the word 'wave' is used in everyday speech for water that is actually moving, as in a wave breaking on a beach.
misconceptions.correction: A floating ball shows what the water does: it bobs up and down in the same place as ripple after ripple passes under it, and is not carried to the far bank. Only the ripple crosses the pond.

misconceptions.question: What is a sound wave in air?
misconceptions.correct: A longitudinal wave of compressions and rarefactions passing through the air.
misconceptions.misconception: Sound is a stream of air that is blown out from the source and travels to your ear.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sound comes from something moving, and it is easy to picture the movement as air being pushed all the way from the source to the listener.
misconceptions.correction: If air travelled from the source to the listener there would be a wind from every sound source and the air by it would run out. Neither happens: the air vibrates in place and passes the wave on.

misconceptions.question: In a longitudinal wave on a slinky, what do the coils do?
misconceptions.correct: Each coil vibrates back and forth about its own position along the slinky.
misconceptions.misconception: The coils travel along the slinky from one end to the other with the wave.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The compressions really do travel the length of the slinky, and it is hard to see that the material forming them changes as they go.
misconceptions.correction: Watch one marked coil: it moves back and forth a short distance and returns, while compressions carry on past it to the far end. The wave travels; the coils do not.

misconceptions.question: How do you tell a transverse wave from a longitudinal wave?
misconceptions.correct: Compare the direction of the oscillations with the direction the wave travels.
misconceptions.misconception: Transverse waves always oscillate up and down, and longitudinal waves oscillate from side to side.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Nearly every textbook picture shows a transverse wave drawn across the page with the oscillations vertical, so 'up and down' gets learned instead of 'at right angles'.
misconceptions.correction: A rope hanging down and shaken sideways carries a transverse wave: the oscillation is horizontal and the wave goes up. What matters is the angle between the two directions, not which way is up.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the particles in a compression?
misconceptions.correct: The particles are pushed closer together, so that region is denser than normal.
misconceptions.misconception: The particles themselves are squashed and become smaller in a compression.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'compression' is used in everyday life for squashing an object, such as a sponge, so it is applied to the particles rather than to the spaces between them.
misconceptions.correction: Particles cannot be squashed. What changes is their spacing: in a compression they are closer together, in a rarefaction further apart, and the particles themselves are unchanged.

misconceptions.question: What is there in a rarefaction?
misconceptions.correct: The same particles as everywhere else, just spread further apart than normal.
misconceptions.misconception: A rarefaction is an empty space, a small vacuum with no particles in it at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Rarefaction' is an unfamiliar word, and diagrams drawn as rows of dots leave visible gaps that look like empty regions.
misconceptions.correction: A rarefaction still contains particles; the density and pressure there are simply lower than normal. Nothing about a sound wave in air removes the air from a region.

misconceptions.question: Are sound waves transverse or longitudinal?
misconceptions.correct: Sound waves travelling through air are longitudinal waves.
misconceptions.misconception: Sound is transverse, because a sound on an oscilloscope screen is drawn as a wavy line.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The trace on an oscilloscope and the wavy line in a diagram are graphs of how pressure changes; students read them as a picture of the wave's shape in space.
misconceptions.correction: The wavy line is a graph, not a photograph of the air. In the air itself the particles vibrate along the direction the sound travels, which makes sound longitudinal.

misconceptions.question: Can a wave be anything other than transverse?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Waves may be either transverse or longitudinal.
misconceptions.misconception: All waves are transverse, because a wave has to have the wavy shape you see in pictures.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The first waves met in science are drawn as curves, and the everyday image of a wave is a hump of water, so the transverse picture becomes the definition of a wave.
misconceptions.correction: Sound in air is longitudinal: it has no wavy shape in space at all, only compressions and rarefactions. Every wave in this topic is one type or the other.

misconceptions.question: Are the particles in a compression moving?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. They are vibrating back and forth about their own fixed positions.
misconceptions.misconception: In a compression the particles are packed tight and held still while the wave moves on.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Static diagrams show compressions as fixed clusters of dots, so the particles look frozen in place rather than vibrating.
misconceptions.correction: The particles keep vibrating all the time. A compression forms where the vibrations happen to bring particles close together, and the region of crowding moves on as they carry on vibrating.

misconceptions.question: How fast do the particles move compared with the wave?
misconceptions.correct: The wave travels much faster and much further than any individual particle moves.
misconceptions.misconception: The particles travel along at the same speed and in the same direction as the wave.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The wave is described as 'moving through the material', which sounds as though the material is moving with it at the same rate.
misconceptions.correction: A ripple crosses a whole pond while a floating ball moves only a few centimetres up and down. The disturbance is passed from particle to particle, so it can travel far further than any particle does.

misconceptions.question: Why are ripples on a water surface transverse?
misconceptions.correct: Because the surface oscillates up and down while the ripple travels outwards.
misconceptions.misconception: Ripples are longitudinal, because the water is pushed outwards from where the stone landed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The ripples clearly spread outwards from the source, and 'pushed outwards' sounds like the pushing that makes a compression in a longitudinal wave.
misconceptions.correction: Spreading outwards is the direction the wave travels, not the direction of the oscillation. The oscillation is up and down, at right angles to that, so the ripples are transverse.

misconceptions.question: What is happening in the gaps between compressions?
misconceptions.correct: Those regions are rarefactions, where the particles are further apart than normal.
misconceptions.misconception: The gaps between compressions are just empty spaces where nothing is going on.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Compressions are the striking feature of diagrams, so the regions between them are read as background rather than as a part of the wave.
misconceptions.correction: A longitudinal wave shows areas of compression and rarefaction. The rarefactions are as much a part of the wave as the compressions and carry the lower pressure of it.

misconceptions.question: What decides whether a wave is transverse or longitudinal?
misconceptions.correct: The direction of the oscillations compared with the direction of travel decides it.
misconceptions.misconception: It depends on how the wave is drawn: curvy lines are transverse, rows of dots are longitudinal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two types are usually introduced through their standard diagrams, so the diagram style is remembered as the definition instead of as a way of representing it.
misconceptions.correction: The same longitudinal wave can be drawn as rows of dots or as a graph shaped like a curve. What classifies it is the physical behaviour of the material, not the choice of diagram.

misconceptions.question: Which direction do you look at to classify a wave?
misconceptions.correct: Both: the oscillation direction is compared with the direction of travel.
misconceptions.misconception: It is the direction the wave travels in that decides which type of wave it is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Longitudinal' sounds like 'along', so students match it to a wave that travels along something such as a rope or a slinky.
misconceptions.correction: A rope can carry either type. Shake the end sideways and the wave is transverse; push and pull the end along the rope and it is longitudinal. Only the oscillation direction differs.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the types of wave is correct?

options.text: All waves are transverse, as diagrams show.
options.rationale: Chosen by students whose mental image of a wave is the wavy curve, so every wave must be transverse.

options.text: The type depends on how the wave is drawn.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who learned the two types from their standard diagrams and treat the diagram style as the definition.

options.text: Water waves are the only transverse waves.
options.rationale: Ripples are given as the example of a transverse wave, so students take the example to be the only case.

options.text: A wave is either transverse or longitudinal.
options.rationale: The specification states that waves may be either transverse or longitudinal; these are the two types.

mcqs.stem: Ripples on a water surface are an example of which type of wave, and for what reason?

options.text: Longitudinal: the water is pushed outwards from where the stone landed.
options.rationale: Chosen because the ripples visibly spread outwards, and 'pushed outwards' sounds like a compression.

options.text: Longitudinal: each bit of water travels along with the ripple it is in.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think the water is carried along, which would make the movement parallel to the travel.

options.text: Transverse: the surface moves up and down as the ripple moves outwards.
options.rationale: The oscillation of the surface is at right angles to the direction the ripple travels, which is what makes a wave transverse.

options.text: Transverse: the ripples spread out in circles across the whole surface.
options.rationale: The classification is right but the reason is not; spreading in circles describes the direction of travel, not the oscillation.

mcqs.stem: A small polystyrene ball floats in a ripple tank while straight ripples pass beneath it. What does the ball do?

options.text: It is carried along with the ripples to the far end of the tank.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who believe the water travels with the wave and would sweep the ball with it.

options.text: It bobs up and down in the same place as each ripple passes.
options.rationale: The surface oscillates vertically about a fixed position, so the ball rises and falls without moving along.

options.text: It moves back and forth along the direction the ripples travel.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who have the oscillation direction wrong and picture a horizontal to-and-fro instead.

options.text: It stays completely still because the ripples pass underneath it.
options.rationale: Over-corrects the idea that the ball is not carried along: the ball does not travel, but it certainly moves up and down.

mcqs.stem: In a sound wave travelling through air, what is a compression?

options.text: A region where the air particles are pushed closer together.
options.rationale: A compression is a region of higher density and pressure, produced by the particles being crowded together.

options.text: A region where the air particles are squashed into a smaller size.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who apply the everyday meaning of compression to the particles rather than to the spacing between them.

options.text: A region where the air particles are held still by the pressure.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read static diagrams as showing frozen clusters of particles.

options.text: A region where all the air particles move in the same direction.
options.rationale: Confuses a compression with a bulk flow of air; the particles vibrate to and fro rather than all drifting one way.

mcqs.stem: What is a rarefaction in a sound wave travelling through air?

options.text: A region of totally empty space with no air particles inside it.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read the gaps in dot diagrams as genuinely empty and treat a rarefaction as a vacuum.

options.text: A region where the air particles have stopped vibrating for now.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think the particles come to rest between compressions.

options.text: A region where the air particles are further apart than normal.
options.rationale: A rarefaction is a region of lower density and pressure, with the particles more spread out.

options.text: A region where the air particles have expanded to a larger size.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think the particles themselves change size rather than their spacing.

mcqs.stem: A loudspeaker cone moves forwards and backwards. What does this produce in the air in front of it?

options.text: A stream of air pushed out from the cone towards the listener.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think sound is moving air rather than a wave passing through it.

options.text: Compressions and rarefactions travelling outwards through the air.
options.rationale: A longitudinal sound wave shows areas of compression and rarefaction, sent out as the cone pushes and pulls the air.

options.text: Side-to-side ripples in the air, like ripples on a water surface.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who take the wavy line used to represent sound as a picture of the air itself.

options.text: Compressions only, with undisturbed air in the gaps between.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who see the compressions as the wave and the regions between them as nothing.

mcqs.stem: How do the density and pressure of the air compare in a compression and in a rarefaction?

options.text: Both are higher in a compression and lower in a rarefaction.
options.rationale: Crowding the particles together raises the density and pressure; spreading them apart lowers both.

options.text: Both stay the same, since only the spacing of particles changes.
options.rationale: Misses that the density of a region is set by how closely its particles are spaced, so spacing and density cannot change separately.

options.text: Air pressure is higher in a compression; a rarefaction has none.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat a rarefaction as an empty region, which would have no pressure at all.

options.text: Density is unchanged because the particles change in size only.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who believe compression shrinks the particles rather than closing the gaps between them.

mcqs.stem: In a transverse wave, how do the oscillations compare with the direction the wave travels?

options.text: They are always up and down, whichever way the wave goes.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who remember the standard picture rather than the relationship between the two directions.

options.text: They are at right angles to the direction the wave travels.
options.rationale: This is the defining property of a transverse wave: oscillation perpendicular to the direction of travel.

options.text: They are along the direction the wave travels, as in sound.
options.rationale: Describes a longitudinal wave; chosen by students who have the two types the wrong way round.

options.text: They are in a circle around the direction the wave travels.
options.rationale: Invents a third arrangement from the circular spreading of ripples seen from above.

mcqs.stem: A rope hangs down from a hook. A student shakes the bottom end from side to side and a wave travels up the rope. Which type of wave is it?

options.text: Transverse, because the oscillation is at right angles to the travel.
options.rationale: The rope moves horizontally while the wave moves vertically, so the two directions are perpendicular.

options.text: Longitudinal, because the movement is sideways here, not up and down.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who classify by absolute directions, treating 'up and down' as the mark of a transverse wave.

options.text: Longitudinal, because the wave travels along the length of the rope.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who match 'longitudinal' to 'along', classifying by the direction of travel alone.

options.text: Transverse, because a rope is only ever able to carry that type.
options.rationale: Right answer, wrong reason: a rope pushed and pulled along its length would carry a longitudinal wave.

mcqs.stem: A slinky lying on a bench is pushed and pulled along its own length. Which description of the wave that travels along it is correct?

options.text: Coils travel from one end of the slinky to the other with the wave.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who see the compressions move and assume the material moves with them.

options.text: Coils vibrate up and down, so this must be a transverse wave instead.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who default to the transverse picture whenever a wave is described as travelling along something.

options.text: Coils vibrate along the slinky, making compressions and rarefactions.
options.rationale: The oscillation is parallel to the direction of travel, which is what produces the areas of compression and rarefaction.

options.text: Coils stay still while compressions move along the slinky past them.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who picture compressions as regions that slide through stationary material.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is evidence that it is the sound wave, and not the air, that crosses a room?

options.text: A loudspeaker blows dust off its cone when the volume is high.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think sound is moving air and look for evidence that air is pushed out.

options.text: Each air particle travels from the loudspeaker to the listener.
options.rationale: States the misconception itself; chosen by students who believe the particles make the journey.

options.text: Turning the volume up makes the loudspeaker cone move further.
options.rationale: A true observation, but it says nothing about whether the air itself travels across the room.

options.text: You can hear a distant loudspeaker with no draught reaching you.
options.rationale: Air arriving from the loudspeaker would be felt as a wind; the sound arrives and the air does not.

mcqs.stem: Ripples cross a pond and reach the far bank. What does this tell you about the water in the pond?

options.text: The water at the near bank has moved across to the far bank now.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think the wave carries the water along with it.

options.text: The water moves across the pond at the same speed as the ripple.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume the material must travel with the wave and at its speed.

options.text: The water level at the far bank rises for good as ripples arrive.
options.rationale: Follows from the idea that water is delivered by each ripple, which would make the level climb steadily.

options.text: Each part of the surface moves up and down as the ripple goes by.
options.rationale: The disturbance is passed on from one part of the surface to the next, so each part only oscillates in place.

mcqs.stem: Suppose the air really did travel along with a sound wave. What would a listener notice?

options.text: Nothing new at all, because sound already is a movement of air.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who equate sound with moving air and so see nothing to test.

options.text: Each particle vibrating about a fixed point, just as it does now.
options.rationale: Describes what actually happens rather than the counterfactual, and is chosen by students who muddle the two.

options.text: Every sound getting steadily louder as it moved from the source.
options.rationale: Plausible-sounding but unconnected: loudness falls with distance whether or not the air travels.

options.text: A wind blowing out from the source whenever a sound was made.
options.rationale: Air moving from source to listener is a flow of air, which is exactly what a wind is; no such wind is observed.

mcqs.stem: Sound travelling through air is compared with ripples on a water surface. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Sound oscillates along its direction of travel; ripples oscillate across it.
options.rationale: Sound in air is longitudinal and ripples on water are transverse, which is precisely this difference.

options.text: Both are transverse waves, because both can be drawn as a wavy curve.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who classify from the diagram rather than from the movement of the material.

options.text: Both are longitudinal waves, because both spread outwards from a source.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who use the direction of spreading instead of the direction of oscillation.

options.text: Ripples oscillate along their travel; sound oscillates across its travel.
options.rationale: The two types swapped over, chosen by students who cannot recall which example goes with which.
